## What are we trying to understand?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson power-lesson"><p>Suppose a researcher compares average scores on a hypothetical attention test with a reference population mean of 50. In our previous activity, we calculated a p-value for a particular observed sample mean. Now imagine planning the study <em>before</em> collecting any data. How often would our test detect a real difference? How often might it make a mistake?</p><p>This optional Week 8 activity uses a two-sided, one-sample z-test with a known population standard deviation. We compare two hypothetical worlds: one where the mean really is 50, and one where the mean differs by a specified amount. Showing both worlds lets us see the consequences of the decision rule. This comparison does not establish a causal treatment effect.</p><div class="clt-overview"><p><strong>Learning goals</strong></p><ol><li>Distinguish Type I and Type II errors from correct statistical decisions.</li><li>Interpret statistical power as the probability of detecting a specified real effect.</li><li>Explain how sample size, effect size and variability influence power.</li><li>Explain the trade-off between the significance level, false positives and power.</li></ol><p><strong>Before starting:</strong> Review sampling distributions, standard error, the null hypothesis, and two-sided p-values from Weeks 6–8.</p></div></div>
~~~

## Make a prediction

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson power-lesson" id="power-lesson"><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="prediction"><legend>If the population mean really differs from 50, what happens to the chance of detecting that difference as sample size increases?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-prediction" value="higher"> It increases.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-prediction" value="same"> It stays the same.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-prediction" value="lower"> It decreases.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check prediction</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="power-explore"><h2 id="power-explore">Explore the consequences of a statistical decision</h2><p><strong>Null hypothesis (H₀):</strong> population mean = 50. <strong>Alternative hypothesis (H₁):</strong> population mean ≠ 50.</p><p class="clt-lead">Choose a study design and a particular true difference to explore. The same two-sided rejection rule applies to both scenarios.</p><div class="clt-controls"><div class="clt-control"><label for="power-n">Observations per study (n)</label><select id="power-n" aria-describedby="power-n-help"><option value="10">10</option><option value="25" selected>25</option><option value="50">50</option><option value="100">100</option></select><span class="clt-help" id="power-n-help">More observations reduce the standard error.</span></div><div class="clt-control"><label for="power-delta">True difference from 50 (score points)</label><select id="power-delta" aria-describedby="power-delta-help"><option value="1">+1 points</option><option value="2">+2 points</option><option value="3">+3 points</option><option value="4" selected>+4 points</option><option value="5">+5 points</option><option value="6">+6 points</option><option value="7">+7 points</option><option value="8">+8 points</option></select><span class="clt-help" id="power-delta-help">The specified alternative mean is 50 plus this difference.</span></div><div class="clt-control"><label for="power-sd">Known population standard deviation (σ)</label><select id="power-sd" aria-describedby="power-sd-help"><option value="5">5</option><option value="10" selected>10</option><option value="15">15</option><option value="20">20</option></select><span class="clt-help" id="power-sd-help">Both populations have the same SD; greater variability makes a fixed difference harder to detect.</span></div><div class="clt-control"><label for="power-alpha">Significance level (α)</label><select id="power-alpha" aria-describedby="power-alpha-help"><option value="0.01">0.01</option><option value="0.05" selected>0.05</option><option value="0.1">0.10</option></select><span class="clt-help" id="power-alpha-help">Choose alpha before seeing data in an actual study.</span></div></div><p class="clt-help">Changing any setting clears the simulated studies so the observed rates match the current model.</p><div class="power-metrics"><div class="power-metric"><span>Type I error (α)</span><strong data-output="alpha">—</strong></div><div class="power-metric"><span>Type II error (β)</span><strong data-output="beta">—</strong></div><div class="power-metric"><span>Statistical power (1 − β)</span><strong data-output="power">—</strong></div></div><h3>Two possible worlds, one decision rule</h3><div class="power-chart-wrap" data-chart="distributions"></div><div class="power-legend"><span><i class="power-key power-good" aria-hidden="true"></i>Correct decision</span><span><i class="power-key power-error" aria-hidden="true"></i>Decision error</span><span>Dashed vertical lines: rejection boundaries</span></div><p class="clt-help">The upper distribution shows sample means when the null is true; the lower shows sample means when the specified effect is real. The two tails beyond the dashed boundaries are the rejection regions in <em>both</em> graphs. In the upper graph, those tails represent Type I errors. In the lower graph, they represent correct detections (power); the area between the boundaries is Type II error. The plots share the same horizontal scale, and their density shapes have the same standard error.</p><table class="clt-summary"><caption>Study design and rejection rule</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Specified alternative mean</th><td data-output="alternative">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Standardized effect size (difference / SD)</th><td data-output="effect">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Standard error (SD / √n)</th><td data-output="se">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Lower critical sample mean</th><td data-output="lower">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Upper critical sample mean</th><td data-output="upper">—</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="clt-caption">Reject H₀ if the sample mean is at or beyond either critical value; otherwise fail to reject. The full normal distribution extends beyond the visible range. Probabilities are calculated using the full distribution, not just the displayed area.</p><h3>What happens if we repeat the study?</h3><p>Each button simulates the same number of independent studies in each world. Because the observations are assumed normal with known SD, we can draw sample means directly from their exact sampling distributions. Each draw represents a new study of the selected sample size.</p><div class="clt-action-row" role="group" aria-label="Simulate studies in each scenario"><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-draw="1">Draw 1 study each</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn" data-draw="100">Draw 100 each</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn" data-draw="1000">Draw 1,000 each</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-action="reset">Reset</button></div><p class="clt-status" data-output="status" role="status" aria-live="polite">Ready. Draw studies to begin.</p><p><strong data-output="total">0</strong> studies simulated per scenario.</p><div class="power-result"><h4>Scenario 1 — Null is true</h4><div class="power-bar" aria-hidden="true"><span class="power-good" data-bar="nullGood"></span><span class="power-error" data-bar="nullError"></span></div><p>Correct non-rejections: <strong data-output="nullKeep">0</strong> · Type I errors: <strong data-output="nullReject">0</strong></p><p>Observed Type I error rate: <strong data-output="observedAlpha">—</strong></p></div><div class="power-result"><h4>Scenario 2 — Specified effect is real</h4><div class="power-bar" aria-hidden="true"><span class="power-good" data-bar="altGood"></span><span class="power-error" data-bar="altError"></span></div><p>Correct detections: <strong data-output="altReject">0</strong> · Type II errors: <strong data-output="altKeep">0</strong></p><p>Observed power: <strong data-output="observedPower">—</strong></p></div><p>Observed Type II error rate: <strong data-output="observedBeta">—</strong></p><p class="clt-help" data-output="latest">No studies simulated yet.</p><p class="clt-caption">Rates use all simulated studies in the relevant scenario, not the combined total. Results vary from run to run. An observed rate of zero or 100% in a finite run is not a guarantee about future studies. Each run is limited to 20,000 studies per scenario.</p></section></div>
~~~

## Interpret what you find

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson power-lesson"><ol><li>Start with n = 25, a true difference of +4, SD = 10, and alpha = .05. Predict how often a real effect will be detected, then simulate 1,000 studies per scenario. Compare the observed error rates and power with their theoretical values.</li><li>Keep everything fixed except n. Compare n = 10, 25 and 100. Why does the alternative distribution become easier to distinguish from the null? Does the theoretical Type I error rate change?</li><li>Return to n = 25 and alpha = .05. Compare a true difference of +2 and +6. Then hold the difference fixed and compare SD = 5 and SD = 20. What happens to standardized effect size and power?</li><li>Set n = 25, difference = +4 and SD = 10. Compare alpha = .01 and .10. Which has fewer false positives? Which has more missed real effects?</li></ol><p><strong>Think about it:</strong> A large sample can make a small effect statistically significant. What else would you want to know before concluding that a difference is practically important?</p></div>
~~~

## What are statistical power and decision errors?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson power-lesson"><p>A hypothesis test makes a decision about evidence, but the decision may or may not agree with reality. In actual research, we do not know which world we are in. In this simulation, we specify the truth so that we can observe the consequences.</p><table class="power-decision-table"><caption>The four possible decisions</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Decision</th><th scope="col">Null is true</th><th scope="col">Specified effect is real</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Reject H₀</th><td data-error>Type I error (false positive)<br>Probability α</td><td data-correct>Correct detection<br>Probability 1 − β (power)</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Fail to reject H₀</th><td data-correct>Correct non-rejection<br>Probability 1 − α</td><td data-error>Type II error (false negative)<br>Probability β</td></tr></tbody></table><p>Power depends on the specific true effect, sample size, population variability, significance level and test. There is no single power value for all possible alternatives.</p><div class="power-formula"><strong>How the pieces fit together</strong><br>Standardized effect size = true mean difference / population SD<br>Standard error = population SD / √n<br>Power = 1 − β<br>β = probability of failing to reject when the specified alternative is true</div><p>For n = 25, difference = 4, SD = 10 and alpha = .05, the standard error is 2. The test rejects when the sample mean is at or below 46.08 or at or above 53.92 (using unrounded boundaries). When the true mean is 54, power is approximately 51.60%, so about half of repeated studies detect that difference and half miss it. When the null mean is 50, the Type I error probability is 5%.</p><p><strong>Why this makes sense:</strong> Larger samples give more precise estimates. A larger true difference or smaller population SD makes the two sampling distributions more distinguishable. A smaller alpha widens the non-rejection region, reducing false positives but increasing missed effects for a fixed design.</p><p>Power is a planning concept, not the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true. Statistical significance is also not the same as effect size or practical importance. Real research often requires t-based power calculations, attention to design and assumptions, and a substantively meaningful target effect.</p></div>
~~~

## Check your understanding

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson power-lesson" id="power-knowledge-check"><p>These four questions revisit the learning goals. Your answers stay in your browser.</p><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="errors"><legend>1. A researcher rejects H₀ when the true population mean is 50. What has occurred?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-errors" value="type2"> A Type II error.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-errors" value="type1"> A Type I error.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-errors" value="correct"> A correct detection.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="power"><legend>2. What does 80% power mean for a specified real effect?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-power" value="true"> There is an 80% probability that the alternative is true.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-power" value="detect"> About 80% of repeated studies would reject H₀ under that specified alternative.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-power" value="exact"> Exactly 80 out of every 100 studies must reject H₀.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="design"><legend>3. Holding the true difference, population SD and alpha fixed, which design has greater power?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-design" value="smaller"> The design with a smaller sample.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-design" value="same"> Both have the same power.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-design" value="larger"> The design with a larger sample.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="tradeoff"><legend>4. What usually happens to power when alpha decreases and everything else remains fixed?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-tradeoff" value="more"> Power increases because the test is more conservative.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-tradeoff" value="less"> Power decreases because rejection becomes harder.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="power-q-tradeoff" value="same"> Power does not change.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><p><strong>Takeaway:</strong> The same decision rule can produce a correct decision or an error depending on the true population. Statistical power describes the long-run chance of detecting a specified effect, and study design influences that chance.</p><p>Textbook connection: OpenStax <em>Introductory Statistics 2e</em>, Chapter 9 (hypothesis testing and Type I and Type II errors); statistical power is a supplemental application.</p></div>
